n: Abraham moves south into the Negev and stays for a time in Gerar, a town near the coast in Philistine country.

f.g: A town in the western Negev, between Gaza and Beersheba.
Lived as a foreigner.

n: As in Egypt, Abraham says Sarah is his sister, and King Abimelech takes her into his household. The danger to the promised son’s mother is real, since Isaac is soon to be born.

f.g: Means “my father is king”; possibly a royal title used by several kings of Gerar.

n: God warns Abimelech in a dream that he is as good as dead for taking a married woman. God protects Sarah and the covenant promise.

f.w: thou art but a dead man
f.g: “You are about to die.”

n: Abimelech had not touched Sarah. He protests that he and his people are innocent.

f.g: Had relations with.

n: He explains that both Abraham and Sarah told him they were siblings, so he acted in good faith.

f.g: A clear conscience; honest intentions.
Innocent actions.

n: God agrees that Abimelech acted innocently and reveals that He kept him from sinning. God’s unseen protection guards people from wrongs they do not know they are about to commit.

f.w: I also withheld thee from sinning against me
f.g: Sin against a marriage is ultimately sin against God.
Allowed.

n: God commands Abimelech to return Sarah and calls Abraham a prophet who will pray for him—the first time the word “prophet” appears in the Bible.

f.g: First use of “prophet” (navi’) in the Bible, emphasizing intercession.

n: Abimelech wakes early and tells his officials, who are terrified. This foreign court shows more fear of God than Abraham expected.

f.g: Very afraid.

n: Abimelech confronts Abraham, asking why he brought such guilt on the kingdom. The pagan king morally rebukes the prophet.

f.g: Adultery was considered a great sin even among Israel’s neighbors.

n: Abimelech asks what Abraham was thinking.

f.g: What did you have in mind?

n: Abraham admits he assumed there was no fear of God there and feared for his life. He misjudged the people—God was at work in Gerar too.

f.g: Reverence for God that leads to moral behavior.

n: Abraham explains that Sarah is truly his half-sister—same father, different mothers. Such marriages were acceptable before the law of Moses.

f.w: the daughter of my father, but not the daughter of my mother

n: Abraham reveals that this had been their arrangement since leaving home. The book of Abraham records that the Lord had told Abraham to say Sarai was his sister in Egypt.

f.g: Hebrew ḥesed — loyal love; a favor of loyalty.

n: Abimelech gives Abraham livestock and servants and returns Sarah—making generous amends.
Unlike Pharaoh, who sent Abraham away, Abimelech invites him to live anywhere in his land.

f.g: Live wherever you like.

n: Abimelech gives a large sum of silver to clear Sarah’s reputation publicly. The gift is a “covering of the eyes,” declaring she is innocent.

f.g: A very large amount—a public vindication.
A public sign of her innocence, so no one could look on her with suspicion.
Vindicated; set right.

n: Abraham prays, and God heals Abimelech’s household so they can have children again. Abraham fulfills his role as a prophet who intercedes.
The narrator explains that God had closed the wombs in Abimelech’s house. Ironically, Abraham prays for others’ fertility just before Sarah herself conceives.

f.g: Completely closed—no one could conceive.
